title: Ecclesiastes 10:1–20
context: A loosely connected collection of proverbs on wisdom and folly, rulers and subjects, work and its risks, speech, and the fortunes of a land under good or poor leadership. The Preacher observes that a little folly can spoil much wisdom, that the social order is sometimes overturned, and that ordinary tasks carry danger and reward skill. Both traditions read the chapter largely as shared ground: practical wisdom for living under the sun, with its limits honestly acknowledged.

verses.text: Dead flies cause the oil of the perfumer to produce an evil odor; so does a little folly outweigh wisdom and honor.
verses.arminianNotes: Dead flies make the perfumer’s oil stink, and a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor. Arminian readers see a warning that one careless choice can undo a reputation built over years, and they stress daily watchfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the image how sin’s small beginnings corrupt the whole, a theme Paul echoes with a little yeast (1 Corinthians 5:6). Wisdom needs not only gifts but steady guarding against folly.

verses.text: A wise man’s heart is at his right hand, but a fool’s heart at his left.
verses.arminianNotes: The wise man’s heart is at his right hand, the fool’s at his left. Arminian readers take the right hand as the place of skill and favor, picturing a heart inclined toward good choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the contrast concerns the direction of the heart, the inner source of conduct (Proverbs 4:23). The proverb carries no political meaning; it describes two orientations of life.

verses.text: Yes also when the fool walks by the way, his understanding fails him, and he says to everyone that he is a fool.
verses.arminianNotes: When the fool walks along the road, he shows everyone he is a fool. Arminian readers note that folly reveals itself in ordinary conduct; character cannot stay hidden for long.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see folly as a condition of the heart that eventually displays itself. What a person is inwardly becomes visible in how he walks, even on an ordinary journey.

verses.text: If the spirit of the ruler rises up against you, don’t leave your place; for gentleness lays great offenses to rest.
verses.arminianNotes: If a ruler’s anger rises against you, do not leave your place, for gentleness lays great offenses to rest. Arminian readers see calm restraint as a wise and freely chosen response under pressure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear an echo of Proverbs 15:1 on a gentle answer turning away wrath. Steady composure before an angry superior is presented as practical wisdom rather than weakness.

verses.text: There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, the sort of error which proceeds from the ruler.
verses.arminianNotes: The Preacher sees an evil under the sun, an error that comes from the ruler. Arminian readers note that those in authority remain accountable for misjudgments that harm others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the Preacher names the failures of rulers honestly. Human authority is real but flawed, and its errors are part of the brokenness of life under the sun.

verses.text: Folly is set in great dignity, and the rich sit in a low place.
verses.arminianNotes: Folly is set in high places while the rich sit low. Arminian readers see the injustice of misplaced honor and a reminder that social position does not measure worth or wisdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an observation of how the world’s order is sometimes overturned. The Preacher reports the anomaly without excusing it, trusting that this life is not the final word.

verses.text: I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking like servants on the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: Servants ride on horses while princes walk like servants. Arminian readers see a vivid picture of reversed fortunes, warning against placing confidence in rank that can quickly change.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Proverbs 19:10 calls it unfitting for a servant to rule over princes. The Preacher records such reversals as part of the unpredictability of a fallen world.

verses.text: He who digs a pit may fall into it; and whoever breaks through a wall may be bitten by a snake.
verses.arminianNotes: Whoever digs a pit may fall into it, and whoever breaks through a wall may be bitten by a snake. Arminian readers see consequences often returning on those who scheme against others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers set the proverb beside Proverbs 26:27 and Psalm 7:15. The verse also describes the ordinary risks of labor, reminding readers that every task carries some danger.

verses.text: Whoever carves out stones may be injured by them. Whoever splits wood may be endangered by it.
verses.arminianNotes: Whoever quarries stones or splits wood may be hurt by them. Arminian readers see the honest risks of ordinary work, which call for care and attention rather than carelessness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that even good and necessary work carries danger in a fallen world. The proverb invites prudence, not fear, in the tasks of daily life.

verses.text: If the ax is blunt, and one doesn’t sharpen the edge, then he must use more strength; but skill brings success.
verses.arminianNotes: If the ax is blunt, more strength is needed, but skill brings success. Arminian readers see the value of preparation: sharpening the tool is wiser than relying on brute effort.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see wisdom as a gift that makes work fruitful and effective. The image commends forethought and skill as good uses of the abilities God provides.

verses.text: If the snake bites before it is charmed, then is there no profit for the charmer’s tongue.
verses.arminianNotes: If the snake bites before it is charmed, the charmer’s skill is useless. Arminian readers see the importance of timing: skill applied too late brings no benefit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the proverb points to the limits of human expertise. Even skill must be used at the right moment, and no ability guarantees success.

verses.text: The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious; but a fool is swallowed by his own lips.
verses.arminianNotes: A wise man’s words are gracious, but a fool is swallowed by his own lips. Arminian readers see speech as a moral choice that can build up or destroy, including the speaker.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear echoes of Proverbs on the power of the tongue (Proverbs 18:7). Gracious speech reflects a wise heart, while foolish talk brings ruin on the one who speaks.

verses.text: The beginning of the words of his mouth is foolishness; and the end of his talk is mischievous madness.
verses.arminianNotes: The fool’s talk begins in foolishness and ends in mischievous madness. Arminian readers see a progression in which careless words grow worse when left unchecked.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that folly in speech escalates. What begins as nonsense ends in something harmful, showing the deepening effect of an unwise heart left unchecked.

verses.text: A fool also multiplies words. Man doesn’t know what will be; and that which will be after him, who can tell him?
verses.arminianNotes: A fool multiplies words, though no one knows what will be. Arminian readers see humility as the fitting response to an uncertain future, rather than confident chatter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the contrast between the fool’s many words and the limits of human knowledge. Only God knows what will come after, a theme the Preacher returns to repeatedly.

verses.text: The labor of fools wearies every one of them; for he doesn’t know how to go to the city.
verses.arminianNotes: The fool’s labor wearies him, for he does not know the way to the city. Arminian readers see wasted effort that comes from neglecting basic understanding.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe the irony of a fool who exhausts himself yet cannot find an obvious road. Without wisdom, even hard and sincere work goes nowhere useful.

verses.text: Woe to you, land, when your king is a child, and your princes eat in the morning!
verses.arminianNotes: Woe to the land whose king is a child and whose princes feast in the morning. Arminian readers see the damage done by immature or self-indulgent leaders who neglect their duties.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the parallel in Isaiah 3:4, where God gives boys as princes in judgment. Some read child here as pointing to inexperience rather than age, though the sense is debated.

verses.text: Happy are you, land, when your king is the son of nobles, and your princes eat in due season, for strength, and not for drunkenness!
verses.arminianNotes: Happy is the land whose king is noble and whose princes eat for strength, not drunkenness. Arminian readers see the blessing that disciplined, responsible leadership brings to a whole people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see good government as a gift of God’s common grace to a nation. Self-control in rulers serves the common good, while indulgence harms everyone under them.

verses.text: By slothfulness the roof sinks in; and through idleness of the hands the house leaks.
verses.arminianNotes: Through laziness the roof sinks in and the house leaks. Arminian readers see neglect as a choice with gradual but real consequences, whether in a home or in a life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Proverbs often warns against sloth (Proverbs 24:30-34). Decay comes slowly through neglect, a picture that applies to households, communities, and souls.

verses.text: A feast is made for laughter, and wine makes the life glad; and money is the answer for all things.
verses.arminianNotes: A feast is made for laughter, wine gladdens life, and money answers everything. Arminian readers take the line as an observation of how people commonly think, not a recommendation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that interpreters differ on whether the Preacher speaks ironically here or simply states a practical truth. Scripture elsewhere warns against the love of money (1 Timothy 6:10).

verses.text: Don’t curse the king, no, not in your thoughts; and don’t curse the rich in your bedroom, for a bird of the sky may carry your voice, and that which has wings may tell the matter.
verses.arminianNotes: Do not curse the king even in your thoughts, for a bird may carry your voice. Arminian readers see prudence in speech and thought, since hidden words often find their way out.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see wisdom in guarding the heart as well as the tongue. The proverbial bird suggests that secrets rarely stay secret, and that respect for authority is wise.
